description: Phillip Jones, a retired Air Force colonel, recalls serving as deputy A5 at U.S. CENTAF at Shaw Air Force Base on September 11, 2001. While watching television at work, he saw the second airplane hit and recognized that the attack was not an accident; he describes his response from Shaw, not being at an attack site. He sent office staff and conference participants home, then helped cancel programs, plan deployments to the Middle East, and arrange support and transportation for personnel in Egypt. Jones recounts that UAE visitors in Sumter, South Carolina, were confined to their hotel rooms after being roughed up, and that military transport was arranged to return them and the Egyptians home. He says he worked without a day off for about 90 days, later contributing to planning for the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Jones also remembers his friend Dwayne Williams, an Army major who perished, and reflects on the loss for Williams’s family and colleagues.

entities_and_facets.perspective: First-person retrospective oral history focused on Jones’s work and response at Shaw Air Force Base; he recounts seeing the attacks on television and does not describe being at an attack site.

support.quote: Good morning. My name is Phil Jones. I'm a retired Air Force colonel. In 9/11, I was the deputy A5 at U.S. CENTAF at Shaw Air Force Base. We had a lot of things going on that day. We had a group of people that were in Egypt that we were trying to manage, and we also had a conference at Shaw Air Force Base in support of an exercise that we were going to have in October. That conference included all the services, other agencies, and also people from Egypt and the United Arab Emirates. Typically in our office, we had a television on, and when the first airplane hit, that was just news. Oh my gosh, somebody made a mistake. And as we're watching it, we see the second airplane hit, and I immediately knew this was not an accident. So I jumped into action. The first thing I did was told everybody in the office to go home because, as far as I knew, being the guys who were responsible for

planning war in the Middle East, we might be a target as well. I made everybody go home. Then I ran across the street to where the conference was going on, and I told all those people to go home as well. And of course, then it was chaos in our headquarters. Our general, in fact, was in the Pentagon, and the deputy was gone, and we had a reserve guy who was filling in. And we sat down and said, What do we do next? And of course, we didn't have a plan at that point on what to do next, but we knew that we had to. Cancel the programs that we had going on, and we had to take care of the guys that were in Egypt, knowing that they've canceled all flights and all the support for those guys was going to stop. So we came up with a game plan on how to deal with that, and immediately we started working on orders to start deploying forces to the Middle East. In the meantime, we started asking

ourselves, Hey, I wonder what happened to those guys from the UAE that we sent back home to the hotel in Sumter, South Carolina. So we went to check on them, and they were locked in their rooms because they'd been roughed up pretty good by the local population. So they hadn't eaten in three days other than what they could get out of a vending machine. So we brought them onto the base, put them on the quarters, and then we didn't know how we were going to get them or the Egyptians back because they were not going to be in airplanes flying out. And even if they were, nobody was going to be getting on an airplane with a bunch of Arabs flying back to the Middle East. So we had to get military transport to come in and get those guys home. But from that point on, for about the next 90 days, I didn't have a day off. And the A-5, the actual A-5 deployed to the Middle East to run the air

operations center, and I was responsible back home to make sure that we worked all of the transportation for all the forces and all the units that were deploying to the Middle East. It wasn't until about Thanksgiving that I got a day off. And, you know, those things continued on for however many years. You know the history: Afghanistan, then the war in Iraq. And I was very instrumental in planning that as well. And we worked our butts off trying to make sure that the people had what they needed, where they needed it, in time to get it there. In the meantime, the poor guys that were stuck in Egypt, they had to make do with what they did. And the major that was in charge from my office did an outstanding job of protecting the people, figuring out how to get some money so he could pay to have the support that he needed, because the support wasn't coming. That was not a priority anymore.
